questions.prompt: Is there a defect in how this code coordinates concurrent transfers from the same account? If so, mark the line(s) where it is; otherwise answer that there is none.
The fraud service hangs for much longer than FRAUD_TIMEOUT_S during a call to transfer(). What does the caller observe?
choices: transfer() blocks until the fraud service answers, because wait_for only applies to CPU-bound work.
transfer() returns None after the timeout and the transfer is silently skipped.
asyncio.TimeoutError is raised to the caller, the pending fraud call is cancelled, and nothing is posted to the ledger.
The ledger entries are posted anyway and the fraud result is applied afterwards.

questions.prompt: Why does _track store each audit task in self._pending_audits instead of just calling asyncio.create_task and discarding the result?
choices: The event loop keeps only weak references to tasks, so an unreferenced task could be garbage collected before finishing; the set also lets flush_audits wait for them.
The set serializes the audit tasks so they run one at a time in order.
Without the set, create_task would run the coroutine synchronously and block the loop.
The set is what makes the task start executing; without it the coroutine never runs.

questions.prompt: transfer_batch is given 50 transfers and one of them raises InsufficientFunds. What does the caller get back?
choices: The InsufficientFunds exception, raised immediately, with the other transfers cancelled.
Only the results of transfers that completed before the failure; the rest are dropped.
A list with entry ids for successes only, with the failed item omitted.
A list in input order where the failed item's slot holds the exception object and the others complete normally, at most five running at once.
